ambiguous_categories:
Third-Party Libraries | AI and Machine-Learning Models

Issue: ml5.js, TensorFlow.js, and PoseNet are functionally third-party libraries. Creating a separate top-level category for AI elevates a specific domain of libraries above others, disrupting the structural hierarchy of the taxonomy.

Web API Endpoints | Data Sources and Persistence | Network Protocols

Issue: These three categories describe different facets of a single data pipeline. For example, fetching weather data via loadJSON() overlaps all three: it queries an API Endpoint, acts as a Data Source, and relies on the HTTP Protocol. Splitting a single data flow across three top-level categories creates ambiguity for developers.

System & Environment Isolation: Runs inside native OS wrappers (Electron, Kiosk mode) accessing local file systems, or embedded inside constrained <iframe> sandboxes (postMessage, blocked sensor access).

Execution & Lifecycle Edge Cases: Multi-screen canvas synchronization (BroadcastChannel), heavy background processing (Web Workers, OffscreenCanvas), and continuous 7/24 exhibition maintenance (watchdog auto-resets, WebGL context recovery).
final_thoughts:
Automation & Testing Dependencies (Headless Testing)
Verifying that generative art renders correctly is notoriously difficult. Testing frameworks like Puppeteer or Playwright take automated canvas screenshots for visual regression testing to prevent layout or render breakage during code updates.

edge_cases_unaccommodated:
'- Sometimes sketches communicate with the page hosting them. For example, OpenProcessing's OPC library is used for the host page to present controls for a sketch. While OPC *can* be self-hosted, if you were to take the verbatim source code of an OpenProcessing sketch using OPC and self-host it, the controls would not show up. Similarly, my job involves making animation software where components in the video editor are p5 sketches. We add a few extra globals/functions to accommodate that different context (see https://www.butter.video/docs) which would prevent the sketch from working on its own.
- Sometimes sketches are integrated into websites and share their state, e.g. if someone made a React site where some component state is passed into a sketch. This maybe could fall into the category of a library as a dependency? But it feels like it stretched the mental model of the taxonomy a bit because the sketch doesn't "own" the dependency; the sketch is a piece of a bigger whole.
- Some sketches will depend on specific environmental factors: sometimes specific browser versions have bugs that would break a sketch if not locked into a working version; some sketches might use a library like p5-serial to communicate with a specific piece of hardware that needs to be plugged in; some sketches might use WebSockets and aren't truly usable unless there are other users on other computers interacting simultaneously

edge_cases_unaccommodated: In installation work, sketches often run offline for weeks in kiosk mode, connected to Arduino via Web Serial, projectors or multiple screens. None of this fits well in the taxonomy, since it only covers input devices. In teaching, many student sketches live in the p5 Web Editor, and they break when libraries, CDN links or the p5.js version change (e.g. 1.x to 2.0). The hosting platform and the p5.js version itself should count as dependencies.
final_thoughts: From an artist's perspective, this taxonomy could be very useful as a simple checklist for documenting a piece when it is exhibited or archived. Many artworks made with p5.js are hard to show again years later because no one recorded what they depended on. A template artists could fill out would make this research very practical.
